:::{#def-hermitian-matrix}
#### Hermitian matrix

A square complex matrix $\matr{A} \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$ is **Hermitian**
(or **self-adjoint**)
if it equals its conjugate transpose (@def-conjugate-transpose):

$$\matr{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = \matr{A}.$$

A square complex matrix $\matr{A}$ is **skew-Hermitian** (or **anti-Hermitian**)
if $\matr{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = -\matr{A}$.

:::

::: notes
The term *self-adjoint* comes directly from @thm-adjoint-inner-product:
when $\matr{A}$ is Hermitian, $\iprod{\matr{A}\vecf{u}}{\vecf{v}} = \iprod{\vecf{u}}{\matr{A}\vecf{v}}$ for all $\vecf{u}, \vecf{v} \in \mathbb{C}^n$.
The linear operator moves across the inner product without change.

Every real symmetric matrix is Hermitian, because for real matrices $\matr{A}^{\mathsf{H}} = \tp{\matr{A}}$.
Just as any real square matrix can be uniquely split into a symmetric part and a skew-symmetric part,
every complex square matrix $\matr{A}$ can be uniquely written as the sum of a Hermitian matrix and a skew-Hermitian matrix:

$$\matr{A} = \underbrace{\frac{\matr{A} + \matr{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2}}_{\text{Hermitian}} + \underbrace{\frac{\matr{A} - \matr{A}^{\mathsf{H}}}{2}}_{\text{skew-Hermitian}}.$$
:::
